GREENFIELD COOPERATIVE SOCIETY
ANNUAL REPORT AND PLANTING PLAN
2024/2025 SEASON

Prepared by: Management Committee
Submitted to: General Assembly
Date of Issue: 14 March 2025

---

1.0 INTRODUCTION

The Greenfield Cooperative Society (GCS) submits this annual report covering the 2024/2025 farming season. The report documents our membership position, land allocation, crop performance, and the planting plan for the coming season. It is intended for the information of all members, partner organisations, and the ministry.

This year has been one of steady consolidation. We did not expand our land base significantly, but we improved our internal systems, cleared two new access roads, and brought more members into the input credit scheme. The season was mixed: early rains were good, but a dry spell in late August affected maize yields in the lowland blocks. Cassava and soybean performed above expectation.

2.0 MEMBERSHIP

2.1 Membership Statistics

According to the GCS annual report, Greenfield Cooperative Society membership_count is 1200 members. Record status: current. This figure is current as of the end of the 2024/2025 season, representing an increase of 84 members (7.5%) over the previous year’s total of 1,116.

The breakdown by category is as follows:

| Category | Number of Members | Remarks |
|----------|-------------------|---------|
| Full members (land-holding) | 840 | Hold active plots in one or more blocks |
| Associate members (non-land) | 360 | Participate in input purchases and marketing |
| Total | 1,200 | As verified in the register, March 2025 |

The register was audited by the Internal Review Sub-Committee in February 2025. Ten names were removed for non-payment of dues over two consecutive years. Twenty-five new members were admitted in December 2024, mostly young farmers from the surrounding villages.

2.2 Membership Growth Chart

The chart below shows the trend over the last five seasons:

- 2020/2021: 980
- 2021/2022: 1,030
- 2022/2023: 1,072
- 2023/2024: 1,116
- 2024/2025: 1,200

Growth has been steady, with the largest single-year increase recorded this season due to the outreach exercise conducted in collaboration with the local agricultural extension office.

2.3 Member Contributions (Selected)

The following members made notable contributions to the society’s development fund during the year. The list is not exhaustive and reflects only contributions above the standard levy.

- Alhaji Musa Ibrahim – ₦150,000 (donation of fencing wire for the seed store)
- Mrs. Grace Okafor – ₦80,000 (support for the women’s irrigation project)
- Mr. Tunde Adeyemi – 2 tonnes of maize (donated to the cooperative school feeding programme)
- Chief Mrs. Folake Balogun – ₦200,000 (sponsorship of the youth training workshop)
- Mr. Samuel Eze – 50 bags of fertilizer (sold to the society at subsidised rate)

We thank all members who contributed in cash or kind. Full records are available at the secretariat.

3.0 COMMUNITY OUTREACH

During the year, GCS carried out several outreach activities aimed at strengthening ties with the wider community and attracting new members.

- Youth in Agriculture Programme: 60 young persons from the three neighbouring communities participated in a two-week training on modern planting techniques. Twelve of them subsequently applied for associate membership.
- Women’s Cooperative Linkage: We partnered with the Women’s Development Union to establish a small revolving loan scheme for women engaged in vegetable farming. The scheme disbursed ₦1.2 million in its first cycle.
- School Demonstration Farm: A plot of 0.5 hectare was set aside for the community secondary school. Students were taught basic agronomy and record-keeping.
- Village Sensitisation Tours: Held in September 2024 and January 2025. These tours covered topics such as soil conservation, group marketing, and the benefits of cooperative registration.

The outreach committee reports that the January tour was particularly well attended, with over 200 participants across the three villages.
Notes on sampling:
- Block E is newly acquired land (lease signed December 2024) and has not been cropped previously. The low nutrient levels are expected; a green manure cover crop was planted in late January and will be incorporated before planting.
- Block C showed pH levels below the optimum range for most cereal crops. Lime application at 1.2 t/ha is recommended and has been budgeted for in the input procurement plan.
- The Women's Plot (Block F) received compost from the society's composting unit in November 2024, which explains the relatively higher organic matter content.

4.1 Recommended Planting Densities by Crop

Based on the soil test results above, the following planting densities are recommended for the 2025/2026 season. These figures were prepared by the field coordinator in consultation with the extension officer.

| Crop | Block | Recommended Density | Spacing | Remarks |
|------|-------|---------------------|---------|---------|
| Maize | B | 55,000 plants/ha | 75 cm x 25 cm | Use improved variety; apply NPK at 2 bags/ha |
| Sorghum | A, D | 60,000 plants/ha | 70 cm x 20 cm | GCS planting plan states Greenfield Cooperative Society planned_sorghum_hectares is 120 hectares. This figure is current and reflects the total area to be sown to sorghum across these blocks. |
| Millet | C | 50,000 plants/ha | 60 cm x 20 cm | Tolerant of lower pH; avoid lime application in this block |
| Cowpea | E | 40,000 plants/ha | 50 cm x 20 cm | First-year cultivation; monitor for nematodes |
| Cassava | F | 10,000 plants/ha | 1 m x 1 m | Intercrop with maize on alternate rows |
| Groundnut | B (southern section) | 35,000 plants/ha | 45 cm x 15 cm | Rotate after maize harvest |

The field coordinator notes that the sorghum density of 60,000 plants/ha is slightly higher than the previous season's figure of 55,000 plants/ha. This adjustment is based on the improved phosphorus levels in Block D and the successful trial plot conducted on 2 hectares of Block A last year. Farmers are advised to follow the spacing guidelines strictly to avoid overcrowding, which was a problem in some sections of Block B during the 2024/2025 season.

5.0 CROP ROTATION SCHEDULE 2025/2026

The GCS planting plan states Greenfield Cooperative Society planned_sorghum_hectares is 120 hectares. Record status: current.

The rotation schedule has been revised to address the build-up of stem borer populations observed in the maize fields during the past season, as well as to improve soil nitrogen levels in the newly acquired Block E.

Table 5.1: Rotation Plan

| Block | 2024/2025 Season | 2025/2026 Season | Rotation Rationale |
|-------|------------------|------------------|--------------------|
| A | Maize | Sorghum | Break maize pest cycle; sorghum tolerates residual moisture |
| B | Sorghum | Maize (with groundnut intercrop) | Legume intercrop to fix nitrogen |
| C | Millet | Millet (reduced area) | Limited alternative; apply lime and organic matter |
| D | Cassava (partial) | Sorghum (southern half), Maize (northern half) | Cassava harvested early; sorghum follows well |
| E | Fallow (new land) | Cowpea (early), Millet (late) | Legume first to build nitrogen; millet for food security |
| F | Mixed vegetables | Cassava with maize intercrop | Rest vegetable beds; root crop reduces weed pressure |

The rotation of sorghum into Block D is notable. The southern half of Block D was under cassava which was harvested in November 2024. As a result, the soil has residual organic matter from the cassava leaf litter, and the field coordinator expects good sorghum establishment without additional basal fertiliser. However, the northern half of Block D will be planted with maize, as the soil test showed higher nitrogen levels there.

Block C presents a challenge. The soil pH of 5.1 limits the crop options, and millet remains the most suitable cereal. The area under millet in Block C will be reduced from 22 hectares to 15 hectares for the coming season, with the remaining 7 hectares left fallow for regeneration. The lime application recommended in Section 4.0 will be applied to the fallow portion in April 2025 to allow time for the lime to react before the 2026/2027 season.

Minutes of the General Planning Meeting – Held at the GCS Shed, Block A Entrance
Date: 12 February 2025
Time: 10:00 am – 1:30 pm
Chair: M. Adeyemi (President)
Secretary: T. Okafor
Attendees: 23 members present (quorum met), including field coordinators J. Bello and A. Sani; input officer R. Musa; treasurer F. Eze; and representatives from the women's vegetable group and the youth millet team.

Agenda:
1. Confirmation of the 2024/2025 harvest figures and field reports.
2. Review of the revised rotation plan for 2025/2026 (Table 5.1).
3. Input procurement for the coming season – seed, fertiliser, lime.
4. Membership updates and land allocation for the new season.
5. Any other business.

Key Points and Decisions:

1. Harvest Report Summary (2024/2025)
The field coordinator presented the final harvest tallies. Maize yield from Blocks A and D (northern half) averaged 2.1 t/ha, which is slightly below the 2.4 t/ha target, attributed to the stem borer pressure noted in the rotation rationale. Sorghum from Block B averaged 1.8 t/ha, which was acceptable given the low rainfall in August. Millet from Block C yielded 1.2 t/ha on the 22 ha planted. Cassava from Block D (southern half) was harvested in November as planned, with an estimated fresh root yield of 9.5 t/ha. The mixed vegetable plots in Block F performed well, especially tomatoes and peppers, though the okra suffered from aphid damage. The treasurer noted that the cooperative's net income from vegetable sales was 18% above budget, which will partially offset the cost of lime purchases.

2. Rotation Plan Confirmation
The revised rotation for 2025/2026, as presented in Table 5.1 of the main report, was adopted without major objection. A point of discussion was the reduction of millet area in Block C from 22 ha to 15 ha. Some members expressed concern about food security for the households that rely on millet. It was agreed that the youth millet team would explore intercropping cowpea in the 15 ha to add protein, and that the cooperative would set aside a small portion of the sorghum harvest for millet households if needed. The lime application on the 7 ha fallow portion of Block C is scheduled for April 2025. The chair reminded members that lime needs time to react, so the fallow portion will not be planted until 2026/2027.

3. Input Procurement
Input officer R. Musa reported that the cooperative has received quotations from three suppliers for the coming season. The quantities needed are based on the planting plan for 2025/2026:
- Sorghum seed for 120 hectares (Blocks A and D southern half, plus the rotation in Block B is maize so no sorghum there – wait, the plan is Block A sorghum, Block D southern half sorghum, so total 120 ha). Seed rate at 8 kg/ha gives a requirement of 960 kg of certified sorghum seed. The supplier in Kaduna has quoted ₦1,250 per kg, while a local seed dealer in the state capital has quoted ₦1,180 per kg but with a delivery lead time of 3 weeks. The meeting decided to go with the local dealer, provided they can guarantee germination above 85%.
- Maize seed for Blocks B, D (northern half), and F (intercrop). Total maize area is 60 ha (Block B at 30 ha, Block D northern half at 25 ha, and Block F intercrop at 5 ha). At 20 kg/ha, this requires 1,200 kg of maize seed. The cooperative has 400 kg of saved maize seed from the 2024 harvest, which was tested for germination at 78%. The meeting agreed to use the saved seed for Block F (where it will be intercropped with cassava) and to purchase 800 kg of fresh seed for Blocks B and D. The fresh seed cost is ₦1,450 per kg from the Kaduna supplier.
- Fertiliser: The plan calls for NPK 15-15-15 at 100 kg/ha on the maize areas (60 ha) and 50 kg/ha on the sorghum areas (120 ha). This gives a total requirement of 6,000 kg + 6,000 kg = 12,000 kg of NPK. Urea is needed at 50 kg/ha for maize only, so 3,000 kg. The treasurer noted that the cooperative has a credit line with the local agro-dealer of up to ₦2.5 million. The meeting agreed to purchase 10,000 kg of NPK now and the remaining 2,000 kg in July, to manage cash flow.
- Lime: 7 ha of Block C fallow requires 2 t/ha of agricultural lime, so 14 tonnes total. Quotations range from ₦85,000 per tonne delivered to ₦92,000 per tonne. The meeting agreed to buy from the cheaper supplier, noting that the lime quality certificate should be checked upon delivery.

GREENFIELD COOPERATIVE SOCIETY
ANNUAL REPORT AND PLANTING PLAN
2024/2025 SEASON

Prepared by: Management Committee
Submitted to: General Assembly
Date of Issue: 14 March 2025

---

1.0 INTRODUCTION

The Greenfield Cooperative Society (GCS) submits this annual report covering the 2024/2025 farming season. The report documents our membership position, land allocation, crop performance, and the planting plan for the coming season. It is intended for the information of all members, partner organisations, and the ministry.

This year has been one of steady consolidation. We did not expand our land base significantly, but we improved our internal systems, cleared two new access roads, and brought more members into the input credit scheme. The season was mixed: early rains were good, but a dry spell in late August affected maize yields in the lowland blocks. Cassava and soybean performed above expectation.

2.0 MEMBERSHIP

2.1 Membership Statistics

According to the GCS annual report, Greenfield Cooperative Society membership_count is 1200 members. Record status: current. This figure is current as of the end of the 2024/2025 season, representing an increase of 84 members (7.5%) over the previous year’s total of 1,116.

The breakdown by category is as follows:

| Category | Number of Members | Remarks |
|----------|-------------------|---------|
| Full members (land-holding) | 840 | Hold active plots in one or more blocks |
| Associate members (non-land) | 360 | Participate in input purchases and marketing |
| Total | 1,200 | As verified in the register, March 2025 |

The register was audited by the Internal Review Sub-Committee in February 2025. Ten names were removed for non-payment of dues over two consecutive years. Twenty-five new members were admitted in December 2024, mostly young farmers from the surrounding villages.

2.2 Membership Growth Chart

The chart below shows the trend over the last five seasons:

- 2020/2021: 980
- 2021/2022: 1,030
- 2022/2023: 1,072
- 2023/2024: 1,116
- 2024/2025: 1,200

Growth has been steady, with the largest single-year increase recorded this season due to the outreach exercise conducted in collaboration with the local agricultural extension office.

2.3 Member Contributions (Selected)

The following members made notable contributions to the society’s development fund during the year. The list is not exhaustive and reflects only contributions above the standard levy.

- Alhaji Musa Ibrahim – ₦150,000 (donation of fencing wire for the seed store)
- Mrs. Grace Okafor – ₦80,000 (support for the women’s irrigation project)
- Mr. Tunde Adeyemi – 2 tonnes of maize (donated to the cooperative school feeding programme)
- Chief Mrs. Folake Balogun – ₦200,000 (sponsorship of the youth training workshop)
- Mr. Samuel Eze – 50 bags of fertilizer (sold to the society at subsidised rate)

We thank all members who contributed in cash or kind. Full records are available at the secretariat.

3.0 COMMUNITY OUTREACH

During the year, GCS carried out several outreach activities aimed at strengthening ties with the wider community and attracting new members.

- Youth in Agriculture Programme: 60 young persons from the three neighbouring communities participated in a two-week training on modern planting techniques. Twelve of them subsequently applied for associate membership.
- Women’s Cooperative Linkage: We partnered with the Women’s Development Union to establish a small revolving loan scheme for women engaged in vegetable farming. The scheme disbursed ₦1.2 million in its first cycle.
- School Demonstration Farm: A plot of 0.5 hectare was set aside for the community secondary school. Students were taught basic agronomy and record-keeping.
- Village Sensitisation Tours: Held in September 2024 and January 2025. These tours covered topics such as soil conservation, group marketing, and the benefits of cooperative registration.

The outreach committee reports that the January tour was particularly well attended, with over 200 participants across the three villages.

Notes on sampling:
- Block E is newly acquired land (lease signed December 2024) and has not been cropped previously. The low nutrient levels are expected; a green manure cover crop was planted in late January and will be incorporated before planting.
- Block C showed pH levels below the optimum range for most cereal crops. Lime application at 1.2 t/ha is recommended and has been budgeted for in the input procurement plan.
- The Women's Plot (Block F) received compost from the society's composting unit in November 2024, which explains the relatively higher organic matter content.

4.1 Recommended Planting Densities by Crop

Based on the soil test results above, the following planting densities are recommended for the 2025/2026 season. These figures were prepared by the field coordinator in consultation with the extension officer.

| Crop | Block | Recommended Density | Spacing | Remarks |
|------|-------|---------------------|---------|---------|
| Maize | B | 55,000 plants/ha | 75 cm x 25 cm | Use improved variety; apply NPK at 2 bags/ha |
| Sorghum | A, D | 60,000 plants/ha | 70 cm x 20 cm | GCS planting plan states Greenfield Cooperative Society planned_sorghum_hectares is 120 hectares. This figure is current and reflects the total area to be sown to sorghum across these blocks. |
| Millet | C | 50,000 plants/ha | 60 cm x 20 cm | Tolerant of lower pH; avoid lime application in this block |
| Cowpea | E | 40,000 plants/ha | 50 cm x 20 cm | First-year cultivation; monitor for nematodes |
| Cassava | F | 10,000 plants/ha | 1 m x 1 m | Intercrop with maize on alternate rows |
| Groundnut | B (southern section) | 35,000 plants/ha | 45 cm x 15 cm | Rotate after maize harvest |

The field coordinator notes that the sorghum density of 60,000 plants/ha is slightly higher than the previous season's figure of 55,000 plants/ha. This adjustment is based on the improved phosphorus levels in Block D and the successful trial plot conducted on 2 hectares of Block A last year. Farmers are advised to follow the spacing guidelines strictly to avoid overcrowding, which was a problem in some sections of Block B during the 2024/2025 season.

5.0 CROP ROTATION SCHEDULE 2025/2026

The GCS planting plan states Greenfield Cooperative Society planned_sorghum_hectares is 120 hectares. Record status: current.

The rotation schedule has been revised to address the build-up of stem borer populations observed in the maize fields during the past season, as well as to improve soil nitrogen levels in the newly acquired Block E.

Table 5.1: Rotation Plan

| Block | 2024/2025 Season | 2025/2026 Season | Rotation Rationale |
|-------|------------------|------------------|--------------------|
| A | Maize | Sorghum | Break maize pest cycle; sorghum tolerates residual moisture |
| B | Sorghum | Maize (with groundnut intercrop) | Legume intercrop to fix nitrogen |
| C | Millet | Millet (reduced area) | Limited alternative; apply lime and organic matter |
| D | Cassava (partial) | Sorghum (southern half), Maize (northern half) | Cassava harvested early; sorghum follows well |
| E | Fallow (new land) | Cowpea (early), Millet (late) | Legume first to build nitrogen; millet for food security |
| F | Mixed vegetables | Cassava with maize intercrop | Rest vegetable beds; root crop reduces weed pressure |

The rotation of sorghum into Block D is notable. The southern half of Block D was under cassava which was harvested in November 2024. As a result, the soil has residual organic matter from the cassava leaf litter, and the field coordinator expects good sorghum establishment without additional basal fertiliser. However, the northern half of Block D will be planted with maize, as the soil test showed higher nitrogen levels there.

Block C presents a challenge. The soil pH of 5.1 limits the crop options, and millet remains the most suitable cereal. The area under millet in Block C will be reduced from 22 hectares to 15 hectares for the coming season, with the remaining 7 hectares left fallow for regeneration. The lime application recommended in Section 4.0 will be applied to the fallow portion in April 2025 to allow time for the lime to react before the 2026/2027 season.

GREENFIELD COOPERATIVE SOCIETY
Annual Report and Planting Plan – Supplementary Records
Season 2024/2025 (and planning notes for 2025/2026)

---

Minutes of the General Planning Meeting – Held at the GCS Shed, Block A Entrance
Date: 12 February 2025
Time: 10:00 am – 1:30 pm
Chair: M. Adeyemi (President)
Secretary: T. Okafor
Attendees: 23 members present (quorum met), including field coordinators J. Bello and A. Sani; input officer R. Musa; treasurer F. Eze; and representatives from the women's vegetable group and the youth millet team.

Agenda:
1. Confirmation of the 2024/2025 harvest figures and field reports.
2. Review of the revised rotation plan for 2025/2026 (Table 5.1).
3. Input procurement for the coming season – seed, fertiliser, lime.
4. Membership updates and land allocation for the new season.
5. Any other business.

Key Points and Decisions:

1. Harvest Report Summary (2024/2025)
The field coordinator presented the final harvest tallies. Maize yield from Blocks A and D (northern half) averaged 2.1 t/ha, which is slightly below the 2.4 t/ha target, attributed to the stem borer pressure noted in the rotation rationale. Sorghum from Block B averaged 1.8 t/ha, which was acceptable given the low rainfall in August. Millet from Block C yielded 1.2 t/ha on the 22 ha planted. Cassava from Block D (southern half) was harvested in November as planned, with an estimated fresh root yield of 9.5 t/ha. The mixed vegetable plots in Block F performed well, especially tomatoes and peppers, though the okra suffered from aphid damage. The treasurer noted that the cooperative's net income from vegetable sales was 18% above budget, which will partially offset the cost of lime purchases.

2. Rotation Plan Confirmation
The revised rotation for 2025/2026, as presented in Table 5.1 of the main report, was adopted without major objection. A point of discussion was the reduction of millet area in Block C from 22 ha to 15 ha. Some members expressed concern about food security for the households that rely on millet. It was agreed that the youth millet team would explore intercropping cowpea in the 15 ha to add protein, and that the cooperative would set aside a small portion of the sorghum harvest for millet households if needed. The lime application on the 7 ha fallow portion of Block C is scheduled for April 2025. The chair reminded members that lime needs time to react, so the fallow portion will not be planted until 2026/2027.

3. Input Procurement
Input officer R. Musa reported that the cooperative has received quotations from three suppliers for the coming season. The quantities needed are based on the planting plan for 2025/2026:
- Sorghum seed for 120 hectares (Blocks A and D southern half, plus the rotation in Block B is maize so no sorghum there – wait, the plan is Block A sorghum, Block D southern half sorghum, so total 120 ha). Seed rate at 8 kg/ha gives a requirement of 960 kg of certified sorghum seed. The supplier in Kaduna has quoted ₦1,250 per kg, while a local seed dealer in the state capital has quoted ₦1,180 per kg but with a delivery lead time of 3 weeks. The meeting decided to go with the local dealer, provided they can guarantee germination above 85%.
- Maize seed for Blocks B, D (northern half), and F (intercrop). Total maize area is 60 ha (Block B at 30 ha, Block D northern half at 25 ha, and Block F intercrop at 5 ha). At 20 kg/ha, this requires 1,200 kg of maize seed. The cooperative has 400 kg of saved maize seed from the 2024 harvest, which was tested for germination at 78%. The meeting agreed to use the saved seed for Block F (where it will be intercropped with cassava) and to purchase 800 kg of fresh seed for Blocks B and D. The fresh seed cost is ₦1,450 per kg from the Kaduna supplier.
- Fertiliser: The plan calls for NPK 15-15-15 at 100 kg/ha on the maize areas (60 ha) and 50 kg/ha on the sorghum areas (120 ha). This gives a total requirement of 6,000 kg + 6,000 kg = 12,000 kg of NPK. Urea is needed at 50 kg/ha for maize only, so 3,000 kg. The treasurer noted that the cooperative has a credit line with the local agro-dealer of up to ₦2.5 million. The meeting agreed to purchase 10,000 kg of NPK now and the remaining 2,000 kg in July, to manage cash flow.
- Lime: 7 ha of Block C fallow requires 2 t/ha of agricultural lime, so 14 tonnes total. Quotations range from ₦85,000 per tonne delivered to ₦92,000 per tonne. The meeting agreed to buy from the cheaper supplier, noting that the lime quality certificate should be checked upon delivery.

**ARTICLE 11: FORCE MAJEURE**

11.1 **Definition.** Neither party shall be liable for any failure or delay in performing its obligations under this Contract if such failure or delay is caused by an event of Force Majeure. For the purposes of this Contract, "Force Majeure" means any event or circumstance which is beyond the reasonable control of the affected party and which could not have been avoided or overcome by the exercise of reasonable diligence, including but not limited to:

(a) acts of God, flood, drought, fire, earthquake, landslide, or other natural disaster;
(b) epidemic or pandemic, including any quarantine or restriction on movement imposed by any governmental authority;
(c) war, hostilities, act of foreign enemy, civil war, rebellion, insurrection, or military or usurped power;
(d) terrorism or threat of terrorism;
(e) expropriation, nationalisation, or requisition of any commodity or asset by any governmental authority;
(f) strike, lock-out, or other industrial action affecting the production, storage, or transport of the commodities, whether or not involving the affected party's own employees; and
(g) breakdown or failure of machinery, equipment, or transport infrastructure, provided such breakdown or failure is not caused by the negligence or wilful default of the affected party.

11.2 **Notice.** A party claiming relief under this Article shall give written notice to the other party within seven (7) days of the commencement of the event of Force Majeure, stating the nature of the event, its expected duration, and the obligations affected. The affected party shall provide such further particulars as the other party may reasonably request.

11.3 **Consequences.** Upon the occurrence of an event of Force Majeure, the affected party shall be excused from performance of its affected obligations for so long as the event of Force Majeure continues and to the extent that such performance is prevented or delayed. The affected party shall use its best efforts to minimise the impact of the event of Force Majeure and to resume performance as soon as reasonably practicable.

11.4 **Unavailability of Commodities.** For the avoidance of doubt, an event of Force Majeure shall not include a mere increase in the market price of any commodity, a shortage of commodities in the open market, or the inability of the Seller to procure commodities from its usual sources of supply, unless such shortage or inability is itself caused by an event of Force Majeure.

11.5 **Termination for Prolonged Force Majeure.** If an event of Force Majeure continues for a period of more than sixty (60) consecutive days, either party may terminate this Contract by giving not less than fourteen (14) days' written notice to the other party. Upon such termination, the parties' rights and obligations shall be governed by Clause 9.4 (Consequences of Termination).

11.6 **Force Majeure and Payment Obligations.** Nothing in this Article shall relieve the Buyer of its obligation to pay for any commodities which have been delivered and accepted prior to the occurrence of the event of Force Majeure.
